newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds ease back on Germany/punt worries.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds ease back on Germany/punt worries.

text.p: Irish bonds eased back on Wednesday in line with German bunds amid worries about the German government's gold deal with the Bundesbank, and uncertainties surrounding the Irish pound, dealers said.

"We opened lower on the back of lower bunds after the Bundesbank chief said there wasn't a firm deal on gold revaluation," a dealer said. "And the situation has been exacerbated by worries about the punt ahead of Friday's general election."
The Irish market had seen selling of the 10-year bond and some two-way interest at the short end, he said.
By 1510 GMT the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 30 pence at 101.80 to yield 6.00 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was down 45 pence at 108.80 to yield 6.68 percent.
Dealers said that yields against German bunds were at 154 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 87 over in the 10-year.
Yesterday, the German government backed away from plans to revalue its gold and currency reserves aimed at helping the country meet EMU criteria.
The market reacted positively to rumours that Bonn and the central bank had reached a compromise.
However, today it emerged that there was no formal agreement between the two.
A slide in the Irish pound against sterling yesterday also led to selling by foreign investors at the short end.
"The central bank rates haven't changed much today and there is still uncertainty in the market," a dealer said.

Opinion polls suggesting either a hung parliament or a narrow win for the opposition Fianna Fail-Progressive Democrat alliance in Friday's general election were also making the market uneasy, dealers said.
"A hung parliament is the worst scenario because it reduces the likelihood of firm action by the central bank," a dealer said.
Dealers shrugged off comments by Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn who said there was no immediate inflationary danger and he saw no need for an interest rate rise.
"Fears of inflation...would not in my view materialise," Quinn told Irish radio. "Therefore I do not believe there is any need whatsoever for an interest rate increase."
"The market dismissed that as "pre-election talk", one dealer said.
The Irish market was looking ahead to credit numbers on Thursday.
